record.paper_title: Statements and open problems on decidable sets X ⊆ N that contain informal notions and refer to the current knowledge on X
record.original_question: Does there exist a decidable set X ⊆ N such that Condition (1), Condition (2), Condition (4), and Condition (5) all hold, but Condition (3) fails? Equivalently, is there such an X for which a known algorithm with no input does return the truth value of the statement that X is infinite, while there is still a known threshold integer for X if X is finite, membership in X is decidable for every natural number, X has many known elements and is conjectured to be infinite, and X is naturally defined in the sense of Definition 1.2?

evidence.quote:
Open Problem 2. Is there a set X ⊆ N that satisfies the conjunction
(Condition 1) ∧ (Condition 2) ∧ ¬(Condition 3) ∧ (Condition 4) ∧ (Condition 5)?

Definition 1.2. Conditions (1)-(5) concern sets X ⊆ N.
(1) A known algorithm with no input returns an integer n satisfying card(X) < ω ⇒ X ⊆ (−∞, n].
(2) A known algorithm for every k ∈ N decides whether or not k ∈ X.
(3) No known algorithm with no input returns the logical value of the statement card(X) = ω.
(4) There are many elements of X and it is conjectured, though so far unproven, that X is infinite.
(5) X is naturally defined. The infiniteness is false or unproven. X has the simplest definition among known sets Y ⊆ N with the same set of known elements.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
For subsets $X \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ (where $\mathbb{N} = \{0,1,2,\dots\}$), consider the following five conditions, formulated relative to current mathematical knowledge:

(1) There is a known algorithm with no input that returns an integer $n$ such that, if $X$ is finite, then $X \subseteq (-\infty, n]$.

(2) There is a known algorithm that, for every $k \in \mathbb{N}$, decides whether or not $k \in X$.

(3) No currently known algorithm with no input returns the truth value of the statement "$\operatorname{card}(X) = \omega$" (i.e., that $X$ is infinite).

(4) Many elements of $X$ are known, and it is conjectured (but so far unproven) that $X$ is infinite.

(5) $X$ is naturally defined in the following sense: its infiniteness is either false or unproven, and among all known sets $Y \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ having the same set of currently known elements, $X$ admits the simplest definition.

Question: Does there exist a decidable set $X \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ that satisfies the conjunction
$$(1) \wedge (2) \wedge \neg(3) \wedge (4) \wedge (5)\,?$$

Equivalently, is there such a set $X$ for which a known input-free algorithm does decide whether $X$ is infinite, while conditions (1), (2), (4), and (5) all hold?
artifact.category_tag: Decidable subsets of N and informal knowledge-relative conditions
artifact.status_search_result: The question is posed as an open problem in Tyszka's work on knowledge-relative conditions for decidable subsets of N. Related follow-up writings by the same author continue to list this and the companion problems as open, with no construction or impossibility proof currently available.

status_evidence.title: Open problems that concern computable sets X ⊆ N
status_evidence.snippet: Open problems concerning conditions (1)–(5) on subsets X ⊆ N are discussed and listed as unresolved.
status_evidence.claim: The conjunction-of-conditions problems for decidable X ⊆ N remain stated as open problems.
